title: Byzantium: The Empire That Lasted 1,000 Years

cards.h: The Romans who never called themselves Byzantine
cards.b:
The empire we call Byzantine never used that name. Its people called themselves Romans right until the end. The word 'Byzantine' was popularised by a German scholar, Hieronymus Wolf, in 1557, more than a century after the empire fell.

So the Roman Empire did not die in 476 CE. It simply moved east and lived another thousand years.

In 330 CE Constantine made the old Greek town of Byzantium into Constantinople, the 'city of Constantine'. It sat where Europe meets Asia, controlling sea trade between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.

The huge Theodosian Walls (built in the 5th century) kept the city safe for about a thousand years.

Justinian ruled 527-565 CE. His wife Theodora, a former actress, was a real partner in power. In 532 the Nika riots nearly toppled him. Legend says Theodora stopped him fleeing by saying that royalty is a fine burial shroud. Thousands of rioters died.

He rebuilt Hagia Sophia in five years (finished 537), still dazzling today, and ordered a clear collection of Roman law, the Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534), which shaped European law.
The Byzantines used Greek fire, a burning liquid sprayed from ships, even burning on water. The exact recipe has been lost.

In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, supposedly heading to Egypt, attacked Constantinople instead and plundered it. The Byzantines retook it in 1261 but never fully recovered.

A new power, the Ottomans, closed in.

On 29 May 1453, Sultan Mehmed II took the city after a siege. His big cannons, designed by a Hungarian engineer called Orban, shattered the walls. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting.

The Ottomans turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque. Many scholars fled to Italy with Greek books, helping to fuel the Renaissance.

cards.h: Was 'Byzantine' just about plots and complexity?
cards.b:
Myth: 'Byzantine' means a mess of intrigue.Fact: the word became an insult in the 18th century (Enlightenment writers like Gibbon and Montesquieu looked down on it). The empire actually ran an efficient tax system, a strong navy and excellent diplomacy.

Also, they spoke Greek, not Latin, from about the 7th century. Yet they never stopped calling themselves Roman.

A merchant visits Sri Lanka

Around 550 CE an Alexandrian merchant named Cosmas Indicopleustes ('Cosmas who sailed to India') wrote the Christian Topography. He visited Sri Lanka, which he calls Taprobane, and reported what he heard of India.

He describes ships from Persia, Ethiopia and China meeting at Sri Lanka, and pepper loading on the Malabar coast, which he calls Male. He also notes Christian communities in Sri Lanka and on the western coast.

A Byzantine merchant on Indian waters shows how far Constantinople's trade reached. Its great rival at sea was Persia, which controlled much of the route.

Five things to remember

  1. Byzantium was the Roman Empire in the east.
  2. Justinian built Hagia Sophia and codified law.
  3. The walls and Greek fire saved the city for centuries.
  4. The Fourth Crusade struck it in 1204.
  5. It fell to the Ottomans on 29 May 1453.

Think about it

  • Why is the name 'Byzantine' misleading?
  • What survives of Rome in the East?

quiz.q: The 1204 attack on Constantinople was by...
quiz.w: Crusaders turned on a Christian city.

quiz.q: Who coined the word 'Byzantine' for the empire?
quiz.w: A German scholar, long after the fall.

sources: Cameron, The Byzantines (2006); Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997); Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography
